subtopic_detail: Numb feet and unsteadiness when the vitamin assay sits inside the reference interval
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 66 year old man with four months of numbness and tingling in both feet, now reaching the mid calf, and increasing unsteadiness in the dark. He has taken metformin for twelve years and a proton pump inhibitor for eight.

On examination he has reduced vibration sense to the knees, absent ankle reflexes with extensor plantar responses, and a positive Romberg test. His full blood count shows a haemoglobin of 141 g/L with a mean corpuscular volume of 94 fL and no hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum vitamin B12 is 168 picomol/L, folate is normal, thyroid function is normal, and glycated haemoglobin is 52 mmol/mol. Methylmalonic acid is markedly elevated and homocysteine is elevated.

data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration sense to the knees, absent ankle reflexes, extensor plantar responses, positive Romberg test, normal power
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-170), mean corpuscular volume 94 fL (80-100), vitamin B12 168 picomol/L (150-700), folate normal, methylmalonic acid markedly elevated, homocysteine elevated, glycated haemoglobin 52 mmol/mol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin on an alternate day loading schedule, then continue three monthly maintenance
options.rationale: The raised methylmalonic acid establishes functional deficiency at the tissue level despite a serum value inside the reference interval, and neurological involvement mandates parenteral loading rather than oral replacement. Maintenance continues indefinitely while the causes, here metformin and acid suppression, remain. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Withhold replacement and repeat the serum vitamin level in three months, as the result lies within the reference interval
options.rationale: Serum vitamin B12 measures total rather than active vitamin and performs poorly in the low normal range, which is why methylmalonic acid was measured. Repeating an insensitive test while the cord is progressively demyelinating is the classic avoidable error. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Attribute the signs to diabetic peripheral neuropathy and start duloxetine with podiatry referral and glycaemic review
options.rationale: Diabetic neuropathy does not produce extensor plantar responses or a positive Romberg test, because it spares the corticospinal tracts and dorsal columns. Those two findings are the disconfirming features that redirect the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start oral folic acid at 5 mg daily and recheck the neurological examination and blood film in three months
options.rationale: Folate given when the real deficiency is cobalamin corrects the blood picture while the neurological damage continues and can accelerate it. Folate is replaced only after cobalamin status has been addressed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start oral cyanocobalamin at high dose daily and recheck the serum vitamin level and symptoms in three months
options.rationale: High dose oral replacement works for uncomplicated deficiency through passive absorption, but neurological disease is treated parenterally because the deficit becomes irreversible if correction is slow or incomplete. Three months of uncertainty is too long when the cord is involved. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methylmalonyl coenzyme A mutase and methionine synthase, so deficiency causes accumulation of methylmalonic acid and homocysteine before the haematological picture changes. Neurological disease can therefore precede anaemia entirely, and around a quarter of patients with subacute combined degeneration have a normal blood count and a normal mean corpuscular volume. The serum assay measures total rather than biologically available vitamin and is unreliable between roughly 150 and 250 picomol/L, which is where metabolite testing earns its place. Metformin reduces ileal absorption and long term acid suppression impairs release of dietary vitamin from protein, and both are common Australian contributors. Treatment of neurological disease is with parenteral hydroxocobalamin, loading on alternate days and then maintaining three monthly, and the prognosis depends heavily on how long symptoms have been present before replacement starts.
key_points: Neurological disease can precede any change in the blood count
Methylmalonic acid confirms deficiency when the serum level is low normal
Extensor plantars and a positive Romberg test point away from diabetic neuropathy
Parenteral replacement is used when there is neurological involvement
Metformin and long term acid suppression are common contributing causes
explanation.pearls: Check the vitamin level before giving folate to anyone with macrocytosis, because folate corrects the anaemia while cobalamin deficiency continues to demyelinate the cord, and the patient who looks better haematologically is the one who arrives later with an irreversible gait disorder.

subtopic_detail: Choosing the next inhaled agent using the blood eosinophil count after repeated exacerbations
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 69 year old woman in clinic. She has smoked 40 pack years and stopped two years ago, and her post bronchodilator ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity is 0.58 with a forced expiratory volume of 48 percent predicted.

Over the past twelve months she has had three exacerbations treated with prednisolone in the community and one requiring hospital admission. She uses a long acting muscarinic antagonist and a long acting beta agonist in a single inhaler, her technique has been checked and is good, and she is adherent. She has no history of asthma or atopy, no bronchiectasis on imaging, and she completed pulmonary rehabilitation six months ago. Her blood eosinophil count is 0.42 x10^9/L on two occasions when well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Reduced breath sounds with prolonged expiration, no wheeze at rest, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Post bronchodilator ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity 0.58, forced expiratory volume in one second 48 percent predicted, blood eosinophils 0.42 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5) on two occasions, computed tomography showing emphysema without bronchiectasis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her inhaled treatment?

options.text: Substitute an inhaled corticosteroid for her long acting muscarinic antagonist, keeping the number of agents the same
options.rationale: Withdrawing the muscarinic antagonist removes the bronchodilator with the strongest evidence for preventing exacerbations, so this trades one benefit for another rather than adding to it. Triple therapy outperforms either dual combination in this group. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

options.text: Substitute a different long acting muscarinic antagonist for her current one, keeping the number of agents the same
options.rationale: Switching within the same class rarely changes exacerbation frequency when adherence and technique are already good, and it delays escalation in a woman having an exacerbation every three months. Device switches matter more than molecule switches in this class. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

options.text: Add long term azithromycin three times weekly, given the number of exacerbations she has had this year
options.rationale: Prophylactic macrolide is a reasonable option for frequent exacerbators but sits after inhaled escalation, particularly when the eosinophil count predicts corticosteroid response. It also requires baseline hearing assessment and electrocardiography for the corrected QT interval. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

options.text: Add maintenance oral prednisolone at a low daily dose, given the number of courses she has needed this year
options.rationale: Long term systemic corticosteroid has no place in stable disease and causes osteoporosis, diabetes, myopathy and skin fragility for no reduction in exacerbations. Repeated courses are an argument for inhaled escalation, not for continuous oral steroid. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

options.text: Add an inhaled corticosteroid to her current two agents, moving her to triple inhaled therapy
options.rationale: A blood eosinophil count of 0.3 x10^9/L or above predicts a worthwhile reduction in exacerbations from inhaled corticosteroid in someone still exacerbating on dual bronchodilation. Her frequent exacerbations and hospital admission make that benefit likely to outweigh the pneumonia risk. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

explanation.summary: Inhaled corticosteroid in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is not for everyone: it reduces exacerbations in some patients and raises the risk of pneumonia in all of them, so selection matters. The blood eosinophil count has emerged as the practical biomarker, with little benefit below 0.1 x10^9/L, uncertain benefit between 0.1 and 0.3, and a clear reduction in exacerbations at 0.3 x10^9/L and above. Australian practice escalates from a single long acting bronchodilator, to dual bronchodilation, to triple therapy in patients who continue to exacerbate, and adds the corticosteroid on the basis of exacerbation frequency and eosinophil count rather than symptom burden alone. Before escalating, adherence, inhaler technique, smoking status, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation and alternative diagnoses such as bronchiectasis and heart failure should all be reviewed, since each is a commoner reason for apparent treatment failure than the inhaler itself.
key_points: Blood eosinophils of 0.3 x10^9/L or above predict benefit from inhaled corticosteroid
Below 0.1 x10^9/L the pneumonia risk outweighs the benefit
Escalate to triple therapy rather than swapping one agent for another
Check adherence, technique and alternative diagnoses before escalating
Prophylactic macrolide is a later option requiring hearing and cardiac screening
explanation.pearls: Recheck the eosinophil count when the patient is well and off systemic corticosteroid, because a sample taken during an exacerbation or within weeks of a prednisolone course is suppressed and will wrongly place a steroid responsive patient in the group predicted not to benefit.

subtopic_detail: Limb pain disproportionate to skin findings when the risk score reads low
stem:
You are the surgical registrar asked to review a 57 year old man with type 2 diabetes who was admitted eight hours ago with a red left calf, treated as cellulitis with intravenous flucloxacillin.

He is now requesting morphine hourly and describes the pain as far worse than the appearance suggests. His pulse is 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air and temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. The erythema has advanced 6 cm beyond the line marked four hours ago, the skin is tense with a small area of dusky discolouration, and sensation over that area is reduced. His white cell count is 19.6 x10^9/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L, C reactive protein 210 mg/L and lactate 3.1 mmol/L. A calculated soft tissue risk score returns a value in the low risk band.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Erythema advanced 6 cm beyond the marked line in four hours, tense skin with a dusky area, reduced sensation over that area, pain out of proportion to appearance
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110), C reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.0), glucose 14.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate surgical exploration in theatre with broad spectrum antibiotics given on the way
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, rapid advance despite appropriate antibiotics, skin anaesthesia and systemic toxicity describe necrotising infection, and the diagnosis is surgical rather than radiological or biochemical. Every hour to debridement measurably increases mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent computed tomography of the leg with contrast to look for gas and fascial oedema before any operation
options.rationale: Imaging can support the diagnosis but a normal scan does not exclude it, gas is present in a minority, and the transfer and scanning time costs an hour in a condition measured in hours. Imaging is for when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and the patient is stable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Escalate to intravenous vancomycin with piperacillin and tazobactam and reassess the limb in four hours
options.rationale: Broadening antibiotics is necessary but cannot sterilise tissue whose blood supply has been thrombosed by the infection, which is why medical management alone has a mortality approaching 100 percent. Four hours of reassessment is four hours of ongoing necrosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Continue the current antibiotic and repeat the risk score in six hours, since it currently sits in the low risk band
options.rationale: That score was derived to raise suspicion, not to exclude the diagnosis, and around one in ten proven cases score in the low risk band on presentation. Using it to overrule the bedside findings is the specific trap this presentation sets. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Perform a bedside incision and drainage of the dusky area under local anaesthesia and send tissue for microscopy
options.rationale: A limited bedside procedure cannot assess the extent of fascial involvement or achieve the wide debridement required, and it delays the theatre visit while offering the illusion of action. Tissue sampling happens in theatre alongside definitive surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is distinguished from cellulitis not by the redness but by the combination of severe pain out of proportion to appearance, rapid progression despite antibiotics, systemic toxicity, tense oedema extending beyond the erythema, skin anaesthesia from destruction of cutaneous nerves, and later bullae or dusky skin. Diabetes, immunosuppression, injecting drug use and recent surgery or trauma are the common predisposing factors. Laboratory scores such as the widely used soft tissue risk score combine C reactive protein, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose, but they were designed to prompt suspicion and lack the negative predictive value needed to rule the diagnosis out. The only reliable diagnostic test is surgical exploration, which is also the treatment, and survival depends primarily on the interval from presentation to first debridement. Broad spectrum antibiotics with anti toxin cover and intensive care support are essential adjuncts.
key_points: Pain out of proportion and skin anaesthesia are the key discriminating findings
Progression despite appropriate antibiotics argues strongly against simple cellulitis
Risk scores raise suspicion but cannot exclude the diagnosis
Surgical exploration is both the diagnostic test and the treatment
Mortality rises with every hour of delay to first debridement
explanation.pearls: Mark the edge of the erythema with a pen and record the time, because an advance of several centimetres in a few hours on appropriate antibiotics is one of the most useful bedside discriminators available and gives a defensible reason to call the surgical registrar back before any imaging returns.

sources.label: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Skin and soft tissue infection

subtopic_detail: Deciding on airway support using bedside respiratory mechanics rather than oximetry in neuromuscular weakness
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 48 year old woman admitted yesterday with worsening generalised myasthenia gravis two weeks after a chest infection. She takes pyridostigmine and prednisolone.

Over the past six hours her voice has become nasal, she can no longer count past 12 in one breath, and she cannot lift her head from the pillow. Her pulse is 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Her forced vital capacity has fallen from 2.4 litres on admission to 1.1 litres, the last two readings taken an hour apart. An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.44, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 38 mmHg and partial pressure of oxygen 92 mmHg on room air. Her chest radiograph is clear and she has no secretions she cannot clear.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Nasal speech, single breath count of 12, unable to lift head from the pillow, weak cough, no ptosis at rest
data_table.Investigations: Forced vital capacity fallen from 2.4 to 1.1 litres over six hours, arterial pH 7.44, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 38 mmHg, partial pressure of oxygen 92 mmHg on room air, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start non invasive ventilation on the ward and reassess her respiratory mechanics in two hours
options.rationale: Non invasive support can help selected patients without bulbar involvement, but weak bulbar muscles and an ineffective cough make aspiration likely and mask ventilation unreliable. Her nasal speech and head drop place her in the group in whom it fails. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Transfer to intensive care for elective intubation, with plasma exchange or immunoglobulin commenced
options.rationale: A forced vital capacity falling below about 15 mL/kg with bulbar weakness predicts respiratory arrest, and the gas and oximetry stay normal until immediately before that happens because the failure is mechanical rather than gas exchange. Elective intubation with immunomodulation is far safer than emergency intubation after collapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Administer an edrophonium test to distinguish myasthenic from cholinergic crisis before any further treatment
options.rationale: This test is obsolete in Australian practice, carries a risk of bradyarrhythmia, and does not alter the immediate need for airway protection in a patient with this vital capacity. The airway decision is made on mechanics, not on aetiology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Continue ward observation with hourly oximetry and arterial gases, intervening if the carbon dioxide level rises
options.rationale: Hypercapnia in neuromuscular respiratory failure is a terminal finding, appearing when the patient can no longer compensate at all. Waiting for it means intubating a patient who has already arrested or aspirated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Increase the pyridostigmine dose substantially and reassess her respiratory mechanics in two hours
options.rationale: Escalating an anticholinesterase in crisis increases secretions and risks a cholinergic picture that is difficult to distinguish from the crisis itself, and many units withhold it during ventilation for that reason. It does not address the mechanism in time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory failure from weakness of the diaphragm, intercostal and bulbar muscles, most often precipitated by infection, surgery, pregnancy or a drug such as an aminoglycoside, a fluoroquinolone, magnesium or a beta blocker. The critical teaching point is that oxygen saturation and arterial blood gases remain normal until decompensation is imminent, because ventilation is maintained by increasing effort until that effort can no longer be sustained. Monitoring is therefore by serial bedside mechanics: forced vital capacity, negative inspiratory force, and the single breath count as a rough surrogate. A vital capacity below roughly 15 to 20 mL/kg or below 1 litre in an adult, a rapidly falling trend, or significant bulbar weakness all indicate intubation. Definitive treatment is plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin, with corticosteroid adjustment, and the precipitant treated in parallel.
key_points: Oximetry and blood gases stay normal until immediately before collapse
Monitor with serial forced vital capacity and single breath count
Vital capacity below about 15 to 20 mL/kg indicates intubation
Bulbar weakness makes non invasive ventilation unreliable
Plasma exchange or immunoglobulin is the definitive treatment in crisis
explanation.pearls: Review the medication chart at every crisis admission, because aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium, beta blockers and intravenous iodinated contrast all worsen neuromuscular transmission, and a crisis precipitated by a drug given on the ward is both common and entirely preventable.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists: Myasthenia gravis

subtopic_detail: A negative early polymerase chain reaction in a febrile confusional state with temporal lobe changes
stem:
You are the medical registrar looking after a 39 year old man admitted two days ago with three days of fever, headache and progressive confusion, and a witnessed generalised seizure in the department.

He was started on intravenous aciclovir and ceftriaxone on arrival. His initial lumbar puncture, performed within twelve hours of admission, showed 34 lymphocytes per microlitre, protein 0.62 g/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L with a paired serum glucose of 5.4 mmol/L, and no organisms on Gram stain. Herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction on that sample is negative and bacterial cultures are sterile. Magnetic resonance imaging today shows increased signal in the right medial temporal lobe and insula. He remains febrile and disorientated, and his electroencephalogram shows right temporal periodic discharges.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Disorientated to time and place, no focal limb weakness, no neck stiffness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid 34 lymphocytes per microlitre, protein 0.62 g/L (0.15-0.45), glucose 3.6 mmol/L with paired serum 5.4 mmol/L, herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction negative on the first sample, magnetic resonance imaging showing right medial temporal and insular signal change, electroencephalogram showing right temporal periodic discharges

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue aciclovir and add intravenous ganciclovir empirically to broaden antiviral cover for the temporal changes
options.rationale: Ganciclovir targets cytomegalovirus, which causes encephalitis almost exclusively in profound immunosuppression and does not produce this temporal lobe pattern. Adding it exposes him to marrow suppression without addressing the likely pathogen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Continue aciclovir and arrange a brain biopsy of the affected temporal lobe to establish a tissue diagnosis
options.rationale: Biopsy was the historical standard but has been superseded by polymerase chain reaction and imaging, and it carries real neurosurgical risk for a result that would not change treatment. It is reserved for undiagnosed deterioration despite full treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Continue aciclovir and repeat the lumbar puncture for polymerase chain reaction testing on a later sample
options.rationale: Polymerase chain reaction sampled within the first seventy two hours of symptoms has a false negative rate of around 10 percent, and the imaging and electroencephalogram findings here are close to characteristic. Treatment continues while a repeat sample is obtained, since stopping on a single early negative has produced avoidable deaths. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Cease aciclovir and start high dose methylprednisolone for a presumed autoimmune encephalitis
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is an important differential and antibody testing should be sent, but it usually evolves over weeks with psychiatric features and movement disorder rather than over days with fever. Immunosuppressing an untreated herpes infection is dangerous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Cease aciclovir and investigate for an alternative cause, given the negative polymerase chain reaction result
options.rationale: The test is highly specific but its sensitivity falls when cerebrospinal fluid is sampled very early, so a negative result in this clinical and radiological context does not exclude the diagnosis. Untreated herpes encephalitis carries a mortality around 70 percent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Herpes simplex encephalitis is the commonest sporadic viral encephalitis and typically presents with fever, headache, personality or behavioural change, confusion and seizures over a few days. The virus has a predilection for the medial temporal lobes, insula and orbitofrontal cortex, giving a recognisable magnetic resonance pattern and often lateralised periodic discharges on electroencephalography. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly raised protein and normal glucose, and diagnosis rests on polymerase chain reaction, which is highly specific but can be falsely negative when fluid is sampled within the first seventy two hours of symptoms or after several days of antiviral therapy. Because mortality without treatment is around 70 percent and aciclovir is comparatively safe, the rule is to continue treatment and repeat the sample rather than to stop on a single early negative result. Autoimmune causes, particularly antibodies against the N methyl D aspartate receptor, are tested in parallel.
key_points: Medial temporal and insular involvement is the characteristic imaging pattern
Early cerebrospinal fluid sampling produces around 10 percent false negatives
Continue aciclovir and repeat the sample rather than stopping treatment
Untreated mortality is around 70 percent and survivors are often disabled
Send autoimmune encephalitis antibodies in parallel, not instead
explanation.pearls: Maintain generous hydration while aciclovir is running and check renal function daily, because crystal nephropathy is common at treatment doses and dose reduction for a rising creatinine is a frequent route to undertreatment in a condition where the full fourteen to twenty one day course matters.
